entries: Aspiring Mangaka is an M1 Merchant that focuses on winning interactions against the opponent by putting them in a disadvantageous position. He accomplishes this by using key tools in his kit. [i]Clairvoyance: Prediction[/i] is essential for forcing the opponent to waste their side dashes, limiting their approach options and making M1 trades more favorable for Aspiring Mangaka. On top of that, he also has [i]Oracle[/i], giving him access to Perfect Blocking and further improving his performance in M1 trades. After winning an M1 trade, Aspiring Mangaka can land [i]Shut Up![/i], which is an effective evasive-baiting tool. It forces the opponent to either use their evasive or take a large combo, as the move's evasive window is shorter than its stun duration, if the opponent does not evade early, they are unable to do so afterward, leaving them vulnerable. [i]Eye Catching[/i] is another defensive layer in Aspiring Mangaka's kit. Beyond the normal utility of a counter, [i]Eye Catching[/i] does not enter cooldown when successfully landed, making it a reliable option for defending against strong neutral tools from other characters and leveling the field. [i]Sacrilege[/i] is another useful tool that benefits from the opponent's limited side dash options. After forcing the opponent to waste their side dash, [i]Sacrilege[/i] can almost guarantee a hit against opponents without a counter. It provides consistent chip damage while also allowing for a combo conversion, as [i]Clairvoyance[/i] extends the ragdoll duration of [i]Sacrilege[/i], allowing Aspiring Mangaka to convert it into [i]Despair[/i] with a side dash.

Black Death is a big-body character that's able to control the neutral at most ranges, their tools aiding them in M1 trading, denying approaches, approaching themselves, and generally forcing the opponent to play their game. Unlike the rest of the cast, most of Black Death's damage comes in the form of their [b]Injury[/b] gimmick: a DoT effect that detonates into instant damage once its gauge is completely filled. Overall, Black Death has a powerful neutral game in exchange for backloaded damage.

Black Death is something that can only be referred to as a “jack of all of all trades.” Each move in this character’s kit can have its own respective use. His unique kit allows for almost every playstyle. Black Death’s main gimmick is that it has poison. Posion can go up to 6 stacks before maxing out at seven, and emptying whilst doing 14 damage. Each poison stack does 3 damage over two seconds,(1.5 per sec, .5 including regen.) Detach a move in his kit, allows for somewhat of a mode switch. However this almost entirely affects combos, unlike Defense Attorney. The mode switch of Detach, in addition to changing the moves, removes the poison stacks, in exchange for more damage. Given the right set up, each move can combo into eachother, and Black Death has a lot of safe options, including movestacking.

- [b]Festering Strikes[/b] can be used up close quarters to pressure the opponent or prevent melee attacks from hitting Black Death thanks to the combination of its parrying gimmick and its pushback and chip damage on block. However, its huge endlag on whiff and the punishable gaps between the swings make it a deceptively risky tool. Use it sparingly outside of combos. - [b]Detach[/b] is a quick poke that's not only hittable at any part of a combo, but also gives Black Death access to [b]Reattach[/b] once it hits the opponent (or, situationally, another surface). It's worth noting that not holding the sword will cause all sources of [b]Injury[/b] stacks to not apply it, instead increasing their damage. It also forces [b]Festering Strikes[/b]'s swordless variant, so you shouldn't use it in neutral until you retrieve the sword. - [b]Reattach[/b] allows Black Death to drag the opponent into M1 range in order to mix them up, making it a very powerful offensive tool; but it can be punished if the opponent predicts when the pull will happen and attacks beforehand, so it should preferably be used after ragdolling the opponent first. Doing so in the air (while the opponent is ragdolled) will fling the opponent upwards and inflict true ragdoll to them during the pull, making it completely safe. It has more utility in neutral when facing characters with certain moves that have high endlag (such as Perfection or True Cannon) since they can be pulled while winding them up in order to punish them at any range. Usually, the threat of a pull will prevent them from using those moves in the first place. - [b]Roach Swarm[/b] is a very versatile move: its regular version is a safe, unblockable, ranged poke that can combo into [b]Detach[/b]. Its R variant exchanges its neutral reliability for higher damage and combo opportunities. Its aerial variant makes Black Death ride the roaches directly, allowing it to be used as a mostly safe (and still unblockable) approach tool that can be followed up by [b]Chokehold[/b] if used right after it connects. - Since [b]Chokehold[/b] can be used at any time, blocking included, it can work as a [i]VERY[/i] risky callout to overly aggresive opponents. It's useful against opponents who don't respect its presence in M1 trades, or those who try to pressure Black Death after [b]Reattach[/b]; but because of its extremely long endlag on block, their opponent predicting this (or expecting a regular M1) is a death sentence. This move is much better suited for combos, especially since it has zero endlag on whiff and can't be avoided with evasive after [b]Festering Strikes[/b] with the right timing. - [b]Earthen Insect Trance[/b], because of its lack of stun, isn't crucial to Black Death's neutral game; but it can be a niche tool against characters with target moves (such as Honored One or Switcher) since the insects are valid targets, and it can sometimes interrupt grab attacks (such as Vessel's [b]Cursed Strikes[/b] or Head of the Hei's [b]Decisive Strikes[/b]) if their users recklessly spin around and hit the insects on accident. Outside of these cases, it's useful for bothering the opponent and dealing some chip damage, but it doesn't offer much value outside of that.

TECH HOW USEFULLNESS/RATING MOVE-STACKING This currently, can only be done with Chokehold. Chokehold has two types of move-stacking, 3 + 2, or 1, 2, 4 + 3. You are able to do this because firstly, Chokehold is green on hit for the player using it, and chokehold has semi no stun. 6.8/10, Dificult to punish if they aren’t expecting it, can also lead to semi-true combos. It also opens up a lot of other various optimal combo paths as well.

Festering Strikes is a really good move in neutral; the parry mechanic grants it melee iframes, and it can be used when close to the opponent. This move can be punished if they block the first 2 hits, but barely anyone can actually do it. Once you land it, if you time it correctly, it's possible to follow it up with Chokehold right after the last hit lands, creating a true combo.
This special variant is very situational, and I personally never use it, but it can be used to follow up with the special Roach Swarm variant and Chokehold.

I mainly use Detach as a poking tool in neutral. If they don't react to it, either side dash behind them to land a hit or dash away and use Aerial Roach Swarm (depends on who you think will win the M1 trade).

If they dash away, try curving it to pull them in. If they block it, it still fills up the injury bar. You can also curve it on purpose if you think they're going to block it, since it will fill the injury bar more. This move can also be used to evasive bait, since if you use it on a ragdolled player, you can combo it into Chokehold.

Chokehold can be used to stun caused by yourself. This means you can hold block and use it to catch your opponent off guard when M1 trading. I only recommend doing this when you're certain the opponent won't hold block or will M1. Other than this, I recommend saving it to follow up after Festering Strikes or to evasive bait after using Reattach on a ragdolled player.

Roach Swarm can be used in neutral and after Reattach since it's unblockable. Regular variant is better for opponents rushing in on you. Air variant is for opponents further away you want to rush in on or to evasive bait (you can pair this with Chokehold for a free combo). The special variant is for combos.

Currently, Black Death's R special is pretty useless; it deals small damage, and the green effect it inflicts barely distracts the opponent. I usually use it from a safe distance and pray it does something (sometimes it interrupts stuff, but it's very weird). You will usually see your opponent exploding the insects on purpose to avoid this (you can't really do anything against that). You can forcefully explode the insects by yourself too by hitting them with Reattach or the Festering Strikes special variant; yet again, this is mid.

Blood Manipulator has everything a great character needs, with strong neutral, great evasive bait, and high damage, allowing him to excel in nearly every situation. Supernova is the defining tool of his kit, being incredibly versatile while also having a very short cooldown. It allows him to completely shut down opponents in neutral, while also having effective applications in combos. His main, and arguably only, weakness is having to engage in M1 trades at the start of the fight to get out of Orbless Mode, but once he overcomes this obstacle, Blood Manipulator becomes unstoppable.

This is Blood Manipulator's main weakness. When in Orbless Mode (typically at the start of a fight), the main goal is getting enough awakening bar to use Convergence, since his damage and neutral are quite lackluster without it. To do this, Blood Manipulator needs to win 2 M1 trades to land the following combos, granting him enough damage to get his orbs: M1 M1 M1 Flowing Red Scale M1 M1 M1 Blood Edge In Orbless Mode, both Piercing Blood and Supernova are too risky for Blood Manipulator to use.
In neutral, both Supernova and Aerial Flowing Red Scale are very hard to play against. Blood Manipulator can abuse them to shut down the opponent and take control of the match.

Blood Manipulator's main evasive bait option is Aerial Flowing Red Scale. Using 3 M1's into this move makes it fully safe, and if positioned correctly, he can pair the orb explosion with a charged Piercing Blood to force opponents to evasive without getting a chance to punish.

The only move to watch out for is Honored One's Limitless special. it can quickly gap close and reduce the effectiveness of your Supernova's neutral game, but with quick enough reaction time you have multiple ways to counteract this: catching with M1 as he teleports, using Aerial Flowing Red Scale to negate the close range pressure, or just backdashing out. Blocking is risky as they can immediately use Rapid Punches so it's not recommended. The only other way Honored One can bypass Supernova's oppressive neutral is by interrupting the throw animation with Reversal Red + Limitless. Any followup is punishable so you dont need to worry too much about it, just be wary.

Pay special attention to Limitless usage, it's his only safe approach option so when it's on cooldown you can use Supernova unhindered. Constantly pressure with Supernova to ensure he can't ever get control of the fight. If he gets through your neutral, use Aerial Flowing Red Scale for safety and M1 trade denial.
How should you approach this matchup?

Vessel simply has no safe approach methods. His Aerial Crushing Blow and Cursed Strikes feint can be interrupted via jumping with Supernova, he cannot Manji Kick Supernova, and Divergent Fist's stun doesnt activate when Supernova is fully thrown out. If Vessel does get into melee range, Aerial Flowing Red Scale can alleviate pressure and let you get back to bullying him with Supernova.

Play passive so hes forced to engage with as many Supernova orbs as possible. Don't be afraid to use Aerial Flowing Red Scale defensively, Vessel has 85 hp so there's less pressure to get off high damage combos. Use your M1s carefully, Manji Kick is moderately effective at combo starting in M1 trades.
How should you approach this matchup?

If Vessel is an easy matchup, Restless Gambler is completely free. Little mobility and no reliable poking leaves him fully at the mercy of Supernova's consistent pressure. Door Guard can't counter it either, and he can't even get safe damage in if he does somehow win an engagement.

Zone with Supernova to make sure he can't reliably get in close. Similar to Manji Kick, it's riskier to M1 in neutral due to Door Guard so be more picky in when you want to M1 trade. M1s into Rough Energy is usually green, if you need orbs you can counter this combo for free.
How should you approach this matchup?

Perfection's only tool outside of blocking to deal with Supernova is using his Blade Mode front dash during Supernova's throw animation. None of his other abilities help in dealing with the orbs, alongside poor neutral game in general and awkward mobility. Without a counter to worry about, Aerial Flowing Red Scale can be used both defensively and as a prediction option for M1 trade denial.

More Supernova zoning. Pay attention for his Blade Mode front dash startup. If you notice slow setup M1s for a wakeup 4th M1 (such as after Stockpile or Body Repel), you can mash Supernova's counter variant for free orbs if needed, although they can predict this and not go for it.

Crow Charmer is a Swiss Army Knife, who has tools for every situation. Every move in her kit brings unique utility to her gameplan. [i]Bird Control[/i] functions as a strong approach and M1 trading option. Her aerial front dash, [i]Flock[/i], is unique, being useful as a quick mid range combo starter that can catch opponents off guard, while also enabling mix up potential if your moves are on cooldown. [i]Spatial Transference[/i] is Crow Charmer's main combo enabler, but it also serves as a powerful mixup option and neutral tool due to its speed and low endlag. Crow Charmer’s combos are more difficult than most other characters, requiring many inputs in a short timeframe. Her moves don't ragdoll for long and the endlag on her moves when whiffed can be very high, but if you can master Crow Charmer's air combos, you'll be met with great reward in devastating damage while maintaining high amounts of safety.

Crow Charmer's neutral revolves around four main options. - Flock - Spatial Transference - Bird Control - Murmurate Flock's usability in neutral varies greatly depending on the playstyle of Crow Charmer's opponent. Against an opponent playing more defensive, she'll have less opportunities to use Flock, as it essentially becomes a front dash that can't go around the opponent. However, against more aggressive opponents, Flock can function as a way to catch side dashes towards her and punish. The opponent being aware of Flock can also make constantly jumping at midrange a viable strategy to keep them on their toes. Spatial Transference is a neutral skip, allowing Crow Charmer to instantly engage her opponent. It has less endlag than Naoya's teleport, while being less restrictive than Gojo's. Having a teleport off cooldown at midrange means Crow Charmer can teleport in front, behind, on top, or to either side of the opponent whenever she so pleases. Teleporting upwards can also be used to escape situations where Crow Charmer on the defensive without a side dash. Bird Control’s directional variants function as a one time use Divine Dogs: Totality swipe. This means Crow Charmer is entirely actionable during the start-up of the move, and does [i]not[/i] cancel upon receiving stun, although the bird will be cancelled if Crow Charmer is ragdolled. The ability to perform any movement or attack during the start-up makes Bird Control an excellent move for engaging with the opponent. Combos into anything on hit, regardless of the directional input used. But Crow Charmer can be caught by an evasive during the start-up of her follow-up attack if caught unaware. Murmurate is Crow Charmer’s most prominent neutral tool. Murmurate is extremely fast with monstrous range, often hitting way further than most expect. Crow Charmer is able to move however she like during the duration of the move, similarly to Charles' Despair or Sword-off Haruta. So despite not having any actual defensive options like blocking, the free movement makes the move far more difficult to punish. This does not mean that the move is unpublishable though, and it is still fairly risky to throw out against skilled opponents.

Evasive baiting as Crow Charmer revolves entirely around [u]mind games.[/u] Her melee moves are rarely ever punished on hit as they're all fast or send at a difficult angle. However, they [i]all[/i] have sizable endlag, a window that will open up Crow Charmer to a punish. This means, if the opponent understands how Crow Charmer plays, her options in baiting out evasive rely almost exclusively on [b]prediction.[/b] Murmurate ... Any time Crow Charmer lands Murmurate in neutral on an opponent with evasive, she creates a guessing game scenario. Murmurate R↑ R↑ after an attack is only punishable on prediction if Crow Charmer inputs a move directly after teleporting. Because the opponent has to guess whether the teleport comes out, Crow Charmer can choose to instead [i]abstain[/i] from teleporting, making them waste their evasive and setting things back to neutral. Murmurate R↑ Air Updraft Bird Control(S) Leads into another R↑ guessing game Murmurate R↑ Circling R↑ Follow ups if Crow Charmer chooses to commit to an R↑

If Crow Charmer lands M1s, it might be more beneficial to go for a true combo for quick damage instead. Requires practice to add Bird Control, otherwise simple. M1 (x3) Murmurate R↑ Bird Control(W) - optional Dive Bomb

Free Fall can steal evasives similarly to Locust Guy Wing Throw or Register Homerun. Circling has massive range and is nearly impossible to evasive punish. It is also the only restand move—moves akin to True Cannon's [i]Unsatisfied[/i] or Black Death's [i]Festering Strikes[/i]—that hits grounded opponents, making it completely safe if the first hit lands. While Impetus Updraft is fast and safe on hit, the moment its hitbox comes out, it becomes unfeintable with Spatial Transference, making it a high risk option on ragdolled opponents with evasive.

Once the opponent has wasted their evasive, Crow Charmer combo routes become extremely free. All of her moves combo into each other and out of each other. It may be worth going for this combo if Crow Charmer's opponent has [i]just[/i] evasived. A single strong combo like this is not main draw of Crow Charmer. Crow Charmer's best neutral option is Murmurate, and that'll combo into any one of her other grounded moves. She has some of the most combo freedom within JJS.

Because of the very small ragdoll duration of a lot of Crow Charmer's moves, green combos become more of a boon than a flaw, something she can take advantage of when moves are on cooldown. Crow Charmer has some of the longest cooldowns in the game. Combine that with short cooldowns, and sometimes it can feel as though Crow Charmer has nothing to do after landing a hit. Fortunately, she can get around that hurdle by utilizing Bounding. M1 (x3) Uppercut (surf) Bounding ... Bounding is completely safe on hit and launches Crow Charmer directly above the opponent. The opponent stalls in the air and exits ragdoll while she is [i]still[/i] airborne, letting her come down in an attempt to get another M1 combo. This is a mix up opportunity that Crow Charmer gains access to every time she lands a Bounding. She can land on top of the opponent and ride them on the way down. She can land before the opponent does, roll, and side dash to get around their block that way. She react and dash in the direction the opponent dashes to catch them. Crow Charmer has a whole conrucopia of options available to her after Bounding lands. These Bounding loops can singlehandedly win her fights. Alongside the Bounding mixup, there are some other green combos she has access to. Jump on the opponent's head Flock M1s ... Crow Charmer’s fourth M1 is extremely slow and easy to punish compared to other characters. Never use this over uppercut. Or in general. There’s no point.
Crow Charmer’s Uppercut launches the opponent much higher than usual.

Crow Charmer quickly swings her axe upwards, launching opponents into the air. This move cannot be cancelled with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] if you miss the swing. Fast startup with a very large upwards hitbox, but leaves a lot to be desired horizontally and downwards. This means just a tiny bit of rubble can completely mess up Crow Charmer's combo. With Impetus also having some of the highest [noauto]whiff endlag[/noauto] of any base attacking move, Crow Charmer will need to be very wary of how and when she uses this attack against an enemy. The endlag also makes it a poor option in M1 trading. As well as the fact that Crow Charmer cannot feint after the hitbox comes out. Impetus Updraft is unpunishable on hit when used out of M1s. It's technically punishable on hit on a ragdolled enemy and on reaction, but it is very rare for an opponent to be able to do this to Crow Charmer consistently. An opponent who knows how to face her will likely choose to save their evasive for more useful areas, like predicting an upwards Spatial Transference. Quick combo that will catch those who are not ready to evasive punish the teleport. m1s (x3) Impetus Updraft R↑ Dive Bomb ... Additionally, with correct positioning on a ragdolled opponent, Crow Charmer can surf and lead into a Bounding [i]without[/i] the use of a Spatial Transference. Useful, if she wants to go into some Bounding loops. Overall, single-use Impetus Updraft finds itself to be much [i]less[/i] valuable to the Crow Charmer gameplan than Air Updraft or double-use Impetus.

A follow-up from Imptetus Updraft. In total, this move does a powerful 17 damage. This makes it the second highest damaging move in Crow Charmer's kit, behind a high area Dive Bomb. Double-use Impetus does not have many follow ups, as the move has endlag on hit, but Crow Charmer can link a Murmurate afterwards. Unlike single-use Impetus, this move can be cancelled with a Spatial Transference [i]after[/i] the hitbox comes out, letting Crow Charmer bail in case of a bad situation.

Crow Charmer[color=hsl(233, 39%, 23%)][/color] swings her axe in a diagonal arc, hitting any opponent above her and knocking them in a arc. During the swing, the move cannot be feinted with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] unless it hits anyone. Due to it's nature as an air exclusive move, as long as it's fairly unwelcoming hitbox, it's exclusively a combo extender. However, by no means is it a bad one. By using it, [color=hsl(233, 39%, 23%)]Crow Charmer[/color] able to consistently link with other moves via the use of [i]Flock[/i], and creates a path to use max height [i]Dive-Bomb[/i]. On top of that, it has extremely low punishability due to it's fast [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]startup[/color] and high knockback.

[i]Air Updraft[/i] is an amazing combo extender, due to how easily it links into other moves as well as it's ability to achieve max height [i]Dive-Bomb[/i]. This key factor allows it to surpass grounded combo routes. Following up with [i]Air Updraft[/i] is possible after an uppercut, [i]Dive-Bomb[/i], [i]Bird Control(W)[/i], and sometimes [i]Murmurate[/i]. Extending after [i]Murmurate[/i] requires the ragdolled player to be hit higher, because if it's used when they're too low it'll whiff. It's advised to stick to using the former 3 options. Follow ups after [i]Air Updraft[/i] are capable of is [i]Flock[/i] and [i]Murmurate[/i]. Both of these require the usage of [i]Spatial Transference(W)[/i].

Crow Charmer performs 2 large swings with her axe. This move can be charged to 3 distinct levels. [b]Uncharged[/b]: Both swings are blockable. The second swing will launch the opponent far forward. [b]Partially Charged[/b] ([color=#fffd00]Yellow [/color]Outline): The second swing becomes unblockable. The second swing will launch the opponent straight upwards. [b]Fully Charged[/b] ([color=#ff0000]Red[/color] Outline): Both swings become unblockable. The second swing will launch the opponent straight upwards like the partially charged version. This move cannot be cancelled with [i]Spatial Transference[/i] once the second swing comes out, unless it hits the opponent.

Combo starting with [i]Circling[/i] is fairly risky. Its high speed and large hitbox make up for it being blockable, but extremely committal on whiff or block. When approaching with [i]Circling[/i], charging the attack varies upon opponent. If they can't punish it in between swings, charging to yellow is recommended. Comboing after circling is simple. No charge allows you to follow up with [i]Spatial Transference (Forward)[/i], then most consistently [i]Murmurate[/i] or [i]Bird Control(S)[/i]. While the charged version can be followed up using nearly anything.

[i]Circling[/i] is best used after a downslam, uppercut, or 3 M1s. By using downslams and uppercuts, it gives Crow Charmer more time to charge to the other variants of the move. The most she can charge circling after 3 M1s is to the yellow charge, immediately allowing a air combo follow up. Circling can fit anywhere in any combo due to it hitting ground and leading into other moves seamlessly.

Crow Charmer flies forward, grabbing her opponent with her axe before slamming down into the ground. The damage of the slam increases when it falls a far enough distance. This move cannot be cancelled using [i]Spatial Transference[/i].

Crow Charmer throws her axe in a circle around her. This move can hit up to two times, and the first hit has true ragdoll. Crow Charmer can move freely during this move, similar to Aspiring Mangaka's [i]Despair[/i]. If used mid-air, Crow Charmer will be stalled in the air until the move ends and will not be able to move freely. This move is an extremely powerful neutral tool due to how much space it covers in a short time, and leads into a combo on hit.

Activates when using [i]Murmurate[/i] above a certain height threshold, slightly higher than [i]Upwards Spatial Transference[/i]. Crow Charmer stalls in the air and slams down with her axe, launching opponents straight into the ground. Upon hitting the ground, the opponent will be bounced back up to Crow Charmer's elevation. This makes it very easy to slot into air combos and follow up from, although it's usefulness ends there. Due to how the move is coded, it is bugged in most ranked maps and will launch the opponent far higher than it should. This unfortunately decreases its combo potential in ranked.

Crow Charmer grabs onto a crow and uses it to hover in the air for a short time. Crow Charmer can move horizontally freely during the move, and can cancel it into any move or M1s during it. If Crow Charmer cancels the move during the flight using [i]Spatial Transference[/i], Bird Control will not be put on cooldown and can be used again.

Crow Charmer calls a bird to attack the player she's targeting with her cursor. Crow Charmer can act freely during this move and the bird will not disappear if she is stunned, only if she is ragdolled. This move has 2 versions depending on whether she's holding backwards or forwards. If Crow Charmer is moving forwards, the bird will launch the opponent upwards and not hit grounded ragdoll. If Crow Charmer is moving backwards, the bird will launch the opponent straight down and hit grounded ragdoll.

Crow Charmer calls her brother to use his cursed technique to teleport her in a direction. She can teleport forwards, backwards, left, or right depending on which direction she is moving when she uses the move. If she uses [i]Spatial Transference[/i] while not holding any directional button she will teleport upwards into the air if she is on the ground, and downwards onto the ground if she is in the air. Crow Charmer can cancel any of her moves into [i]Spatial Transference[/i] (with exceptions, written in each moves description) until they are blocked. When Crow Charmer lands any move (except Bounding and backwards Bird Control), this move will be taken off cooldown. Due to these properties, [i]Spatial Transference[/i] is what enables most of Crow Charmer's air combos. It is also a potent mixup option due to its fast speed and ambiguity.

Replaces front dash while mid-air, and puts front dash on a 10 second cooldown. Crow Charmer stalls in the air and juts out a knee in front of her, moving forwards a moderate distance. Upon connecting with an opponent, she will knock both herself and the opponent upwards an equal distance. This ragdolls the opponent. [i]Flock[/i] is a powerful neutral tool, essentially being a safe front dash, at the cost of not being able to turn it and having a longer cooldown. It also has its use in combos, being fairly easy to slot in to routes and giving a substantial amount of height.

Replaces front dash when mid-air and close to a ragdolled opponent, and puts front dash on a 2 second cooldown. Crow Charmer footstools her opponent, kicking off them and launching herself up a short distance. After being hit by [i]Bounding[/i], the opponent will be ragdolled for a second and be stalled in the air until they recover from ragdoll. [i]Bounding[/i] is an efficient way to add damage to a combo, or to gain height required for [i]Free Fall[/i].

Cursed Partners main gimmick are fast dash moves with supreme block pressure, along with good defense via [i]Outburst[/i] (Parry) and [i]Rika Haymaker[/i], allowing him to be extremely aggressive while maintaining safety. Combined with [i]Resolute Slash[/i] as a ranged block bypass, Cursed Partners has a solution for almost any situation he finds himself in. Rika is an extremely effective assist moveset, working as a combo tool, evasive bait, movement/approach tool and as a reversal. Additionally, having 5 moves along with decent cooldowns allows Cursed Partners to keep pressing the advantage and/or have tools constantly (15,15,16,16) (10 for rika). Cursed Partners is a great pick for offense up close while also having good versatilities in Rika to cover weaknesses.

Cursed Partners excels at shutting down aggressive opponents while also being a decent rushdown himself. [i]Veilstep[/i], [i]Rika Smash[/i] and [i]Second Wind[/i] are reliable for catching opponents off guard, [i]Rika Smash[/i], [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] and [i]Outburst[/i] assures Yuta has good defensive options while [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] and [i]Resolute Slash[/i] enables him to get the offense on blocking opponents.

You can also use Rika Smash (Aerial) on any uptilt move (e.g: Veilstep) 3 m1s Severing Path Rika Smash (aerial) Since [i]Rika Smash[/i] (Aerial) applies true ragdoll and converts into both heavy hitting moves ([i]Resolute Slash[/i], [i]Outburst[/i] (Max charge)), additionally falling on a low cooldown (10s), while also being near instataneous, your opponent will always have to evasive right after any uptilt move or suffer tremendous damage. [i]Rika Smash[/i] (Aerial) will also slow your opponent down substantiallly if they do evasive, potentially allowing for mixups if they do evasive. 3m1s Resolute slash rikahaymaker veilstep Normally resolute slash is evasive punishable, but if you were to use rika haymaker after they've been knocked back it would follow them if they tried too punish you which will lead into veil step, and if they don't evasive they'll still eat haymaker into veil step Rika haymaker on block does 18 damage (and just moves them back instead of knockback which could lead to a untrue mixup)

Cursed Partners combos deal a moderate amount of damage most of the time, potentially insane damage if his variants are used properly and with some sneaky m1s in. 3 M1s Severing path Uppercut Rika Smash (Aerial) Outburst (max charge) Second Wind Resolute Slash (Black flash) A simple, safe yet effective combo, you can sneak in a downslam after [i]Rika Smash[/i] (Aerial) if you are sure the opponent doesn't have their evasive, this combo acts as both evasive bait and well, a combo. Veilstep Rika Smash (Aerial) Outburst (Max charge) second wind resolute slash (black flash) Cursed Partners safe combo for converting off of his neutral option [i]Veilstep[/i], which can be interchangeable with [i]Second Wind[/i]. 3 m1s Uppercut Severing Path (Aerial) Outburst (max charge) Second Wind Rika Haymaker Resolute Slash (BLACK FLASH) This is Cursed Partners main combo after baiting evasive, [i]Severing Path[/i] (Aerial) deals 4 more damage than normal [i]Severing Path[/i], using up a [i]Second Wind[/i] charge but doesn't put [i]Second Wind[/i] on cooldown if you have yet to use your first charge, allowing you to use [i]Second Wind[/i] again. The timing for both [i]Rika Haymaker[/i] and [i]Resolute Slash[/i] to hit can be tricky, but you can avoid this by using [i]Rika Smash[/i], exchanging 2 damage for consistency.

Cursed Partners is one of the buggier characters as of current, having plenty of issues with his moves as follow: - [i]Second Wind[/i] sometimes teleports the opponent after slamming them, this becomes ever more apparent as the move does not mesh well with the destruction physics, making it extremely difficult for, or even incapacitating Yuta from following-up. - The destruction physics can also sometimes reduces the ragdoll duration of Cursed Partners moves if your opponent is beneath debris. - Rika's move slots can become invisible sometimes. Rika gets put on a 6 second cooldown if [i]Rika Launch[/i] feint variant was activated. Do an m1 or dash and then [i]Rika Launch[/i] to avoid getting put on a 13 second cooldown. Ever since [i]Outburst[/i]'s initial slash has been changed to hit grounded ragdolls, the move can be charged up to max after [i]Severing Path[/i] and [i]Second wind[/i], and charged up to 2 after [i]Resolute Slash[/i]. [i]Outburst[/i] has a very small parry window (0.2 seconds, which is very short). But Cursed Partners is incentivised by a 2 second cooldown reduction on Rika, and this variant can be useful against mixups or certain moves that are hard to dodge, especially if dashes are unavailable.

TECH HOW DO I DO THIS WHY IS THIS USEFUL [i]Severing Path[/i] M1 Reset Severing Path > Rika Launch Feint (Right as the 3rd slash hits) > 4 M1s (May need a side dash if Rika pushes you too far.) Improves Cursed Partners combo game tremendously, while failing this gives Yuta the opportunity to begin an advantageous m1 trade at the cost of 2.3 damage. In short, The reward outweighs risk. If the first M1 off of Rika Launch didn't hit immediately, the tech has failed. Practice is needed, this tech is somewhat inconsistent. [i]Invisible Rika (BUG)[/i] R > (Rika) 1,2,3 > R (In quick succession.) Pressing R twice in a row dismisses Rika, but you can actually do a move in between to obscure Rika. Especially useful on [i]Rika Haymaker[/i], Invisible Rika can lead to more value than a normal haymaker by inducing uncertainty to an opponent if Haymaker will hit, confusing them and reducing chances of side dashing away to dodge an easily visible Haymaker. Additionally useful in M1 trading, where a blocking opponent blocks Rika Haymaker increases the damage. [i]Anti-Bleed (BUG...?)[/i] After getting hit with [i]Bleedout[/I], Use any Rika move (Other than feinting) and switch back to her moveset before the cooldown takes effect. This removes all 3 bleedout stacks at once using one move because of the game's mechanics of shared cooldowns on all of Rika's moves. By using one Rika move, Cursed Partners registers all 3 Rika moves going off cooldown. This is useful generally against Head of the Hei, considering Bleedout stacks delay Projection decay and can induce [i]Hemmorhage[/i].

Severing Path is exclusively Cursed Partners main convert/extender for his combos, being unreliable in neutral or mixups due to it's decently slow startup along with a generously long recovery time. Don't use it on a ragdolled player if they have their evasive since the startup is reactable. Jump after landing this move if you want to follow up with Second Wind to make it safer and more consistent. Severing Path could also be used as an m1 reset when paired with Rika Launch (Grounded) to cancel the move before the final ragdolling strike. Be careful as the timing required to pull this off is extremely unintuitive.

Backwards Severing Path, otherwise known as Veilstep, stand as the pinnacle of Cursed Partners neutral, providing Melee I-frames, low Startup and a moving, lingering hitbox. Being essentially unpunishable, Veilstep provides exceptional block pressure as a poke tool. This move can also be used to avoid getting evasive punished, rather than the normal variant of Severing Path. It's recommended to save this move in neutral against certain opponents (e.x yuji/naoya) due to the melee iframes and knock up you can combo into Rika downslam.

Resolute Slash is really good to punish wasted side dashes from a close-medium distance, and can also be useful when done on wake-up as the startup and windup are pretty fast, coupled with the fact that the only way to deal with a wake-up Resolute Slash is to either evasive or use a counter. While the Black Flash variant is what most people would use, the regular variant has the unique effect of keeping the enemy ragdolled longer, meaning Cursed Partners can extend this into either 1 or 3 if Resolute Slash hits. Both of these moves can be feinted out of to remove the endlag.

This variant is mostly useful for the end of a combo, as the knockback sends the opponent out of side dash range while also waking them up once the knockback is done. Unlike Resolute Slash, this move can be used against ragdolled opponents, which is the reason why most players use this variant instead. Ironically, this variant does NOT deal more damage than it's base move, despite being a black flash. The only difference it has is that it hits grounded ragdolls at the cost of being punishable on whiff (And having a really cool finisher. it can also be feinted to remove it's long endedlag).

Outburst is a really safe move; using it in M1 trades or when you know you're about to get hit basically guarantees your safety since it will either hit the parry or the explosion. It can also be used to parry projectiles. If you want to use the fully charged variant in a combo but you know the opponent won't be ragdolled for enough time to land it, you can use Rika Smash during the windup to extend their ragdoll (pairing these 2 moves together is also really good evasive bait, but you're putting your best moves on cooldown for it).

The first use of Second Wind is punishable in neutral, but it's a very small window, so if they're not expecting it, you can get away with it. Second wind also has a really good vertical hitbox, pair that with it having melee iframes you can cancel alot of aerial and grounded moves by doing jump 4 (e.x Crushing Blow/Cursed Strikes and Speed Crash) If you don't land the first use, save the second one for combos (and if you miss the second one make sure to feint to remove endlag).

This move does 15 dmage, leads into all of his moves (including a downslam) at the cost of taking up both 4 and 1 if used, and requires an enemy to be infront of you to us it (also it's a grab for some reason ig and can be used in the air).

Rika Smash is a good tool for punishing opponents trying to get an advantage out of your own mistakes. It forces the opponent to block, so it's useful in M1 trades. It can combo into and out of every move in your kit, you can also use it with Outburst, like mentioned earlier.

FEINT Rika launch is good for movement and canceling due to it's feinting ability, it's regular cooldown is 10s but if feinted with a move, it turns into a 6s cooldown, so always do a jump m1 or a forward/side dash for optimal cooldowns with movement. Feinting is really useful to cancel the endlag of heavy moves like both of Resolute Slash variants, and the 2nd part of Second Wind.

AERIAL FEINT This variant has the same cooldown propreties as the first, but with the difference being vertical moviment instead of horizontal, giving you easy acess to the air. Gaining height like this is useful for some things, like easy acess to rolls, dodging a move or just being unpredictable with your moviment. However, its value is easily overshadowed by the normal variant, thanks to the acess of the m1 reset previously mentioned, and the fact that horizontal moviment has more uses in a fight, and is harder to react.

Rika Haymaker is the best evasive baiting tool Rika has. You can use it in neutral to guarantee your safety while it's active, and because of it's slow windup rika follows people if they evasive (and timed well) which can lead to another combo after you caught them. it does 18 damage instead of the usual 12 when blocked and instead of knocking them back just pushes them which can lead to a silly mixup.

A strong M1-centric rushdown augmented with some of the fastest mobility in the game, Defense Attorney excels at tripping his opponents up with his blistering speed, making them second-guess themselves at every turn with his strong mix-up game. Defense Attorney has a pretty good neutral game relative to other M1 merchants, with 3+R and R+R on top of your regular side dash and front-dash, making his movement way faster than most characters. He also has access to multiple incredibly strong pokes, with two safe pokes in 3 and R+4, and an unsafe but guardbreaking poke in R+3. His ultimate allows him to continue piling on the pressure, either through confiscation or through his awakening. Defense Attorney is a great pick for enhancing and making use of well-developed fundamentals.

Strategy with Defense Attorney starts with you trying to get up close with your mobility tools to net you an M1 string and a knockdown, so you can start your offense. Once you put an opponent in a ragdoll state, Defense Attorney becomes a much more dangerous threat, with his ability to control when ragdoll ends with his special ( [b]R[/b] ). With his gavel out of the way, he gains access to answers to just about any option an opponent might throw out. Your goal is to pick up on habits and respond accordingly, capitalizing on reads to cash out damage, and to keep changing things up until your opponent is suffocated in your pressure.

Typically, [b]R + R [/b] is what you would prefer to open with at almost all ranges, as Defense Attorney lets you manipulate your velocity on the hop by holding jump or a movement key, or even both. Here are some examples: Sends you further R Spacebar + w r (instantly) Hops a short distance R S R (INSTANTLY)

Whilst not being as powerful as [b]R + R[/b] in terms of versatility with velocity, [b]3 + R[/b is a very useful tool with its built-in mindgame, and it does not put your gavel on cooldown. It can also be used mid-air and combined with your other approach options to cover even greater distances. There are two schools of thought when using Defense Attorney's [b]3 + R[/b]: [b]*[/b] Using it to get in and begin offense [b]*[/b] Using it after a knockdown to threaten [b]3[/b]'s interruption variant or [b]3 + 3 [/b]

[b]4 + Any [/b] is a weird option that you wouldn't typically throw out, as it is very vulnerable to getting hit out of, with the exception of some moves such as Cursed Strikes or Flowing Red Scale, as [b]4[/b] puts out a hitbox during the first part of the move. Even so, being unpredictable is a strength that Defense Attorney uses very well with this option, as its variants crush actions and block respectively. Use this sparingly, as missing puts you in a very bad spot.

He can combo pretty much anything in his kit into and out of another thing in his kit, but here's a few combos that you should know. Starting with Defense Attorney's bread and butter: 3 m1s uppercut R (whiff) 4 FrontDash 2 m1s uppercut 1 2 3 R R (optional) Defense Attorney's main BNB. Solid damage, sets up mix at the end with R, and can lead to an m1 reset if you play your cards right. If your opponent doesn't have evasive, you'll be using this combo on them a vast majority of the time. Defense Attorney doesn't have much in the way of actual true combos. The most you can do is 3 m1s into Extended Swings, which is pretty lackluster. Defense Attorney does, however, have safe evasive bait that leads into decent damage; when they do have evasive, use this one instead. 3 m1s 2 backdash + 3 r (whiff) sidedash + 4 frontdash 2 m1s 1 Justice Served into Grapple is the safest way Defense Attorney can bait evasive, so while this combo may not be true, it's a pretty safe way to either deal a load of damage or bait evasive. Bear in mind that this combo doesn't provide any mix afterwards, as your R will be on cooldown.

It's somewhat quick and large enough to use in neutral to catch someone off-guard, but it's also pretty easily punishable on block... Yeah just stick to using this as combo food. It's also a surprisingly common misconception that you can immediately evasive and punish the endlag of this move on hit. You can't. This move is safe. [i]This [/i]move is what's basically the backbone of Defense Attorney's mix. Melee invul, huge, incredibly quick, even hits people who aren't blocking it, and most importantly crushes on block AND interruption, this move is insane. This move alone makes opponents wary when your mallet is thrown out, and forces them to stop what they're doing. But this doesn't mean that you should [i]always[/i] use this move once your mallet is out. A large, common mistake that I see in novice Defense Attorney players is CONSTANTLY using this sweep. Reason being that against newer players, this move is seemingly no risk as it knocks back even when it doesn't crush. But that knockback has no stun (and damage, but that's kind of a non-issue) on it; a more experienced player will sometimes catch you on hit and punish the endlag. Like a majority of Defense Attorney's kit, you should use this move carefully to form and/or punish habits. Note when the opponent tends to throw out moves, and use R+1 to punish them.

A coward would call this move mere combo food. A player without conviction... A player without drive to be... [i]more...[/i] Sure you can use it during your combos. It's probably the most safe option you have after m1s and you can use Grapple right after to get pretty safe damage when your opponent has evasive, and when they don't you can combo out of it with R+4 or 1... But what about using this move... [i]unsafely...[/i] This move has the benefit of being pretty big and lagless for a guard-breaking move, meaning that you can surprisingly get away with using this move raw quite often. A big reason why is because people aren't typically that concerned about getting their guard broken by moves on other characters, as they typically don't lead to true combos and tend to be evasive-able. Justice Served, however, has the benefit of crushing blocks and leading straight into an m1 chain. A lot of the time this means that you can get away with throwing out side dash + Justice Served raw, and since the usual reaction to a close quarters side dash is to block the obvious incoming m1... you see where this is going. This is, of course, unsafe. Sure, Justice Served has comparatively low windup and endlag compared to similar guardbreaks, but it's still plenty punishable on whiff/reaction. But a lot of Defense Attorney's gameplan is messing with your opponents head and trying to get them to pick up bad habits in an attempt to counterplay you. Hitting someone with raw Justice Served multiple times may cause them to adopt bad habits against you, like retreating after you side dash at them, or trying to stuff out the supposed incoming Justice Served with m1s on reaction to your side dash. You shouldn't spam raw Justice Served. You also shouldn't forget that it's still plenty useful as combo food as well, converting off of ragdolls and into every move in Defense Attorney's kit. But when it works... [i]hoooooooooooooo boy[/i] it works. Justice Served tends to sometimes whiff at close range or when debris is at play. Judgement's Reach is a very interesting move. It's the biggest disjoint in your kit, and you're going to be using it as such; it's a solid poke to use in neutral when fishing for a hit. What makes this move interesting is the interruption property that it has; if this move lands on someone who's in the process of using a move/m1s (unless that move is a counter, of course), it'll inflict a long period of stun on that player, allowing for a follow-up with a front dash. Bear in mind that landing the interruption doesn't reset your front dash cooldown, so sometimes you'll have to settle for a side dash and m1 to convert. You can also situationally land punishes after an evasive that would be hard to do with normal m1s; for example, Restless Gambler's main bnb (Uppercut Surf > Fever Breaker) is hard to punish normally with m1s. Judgement's Reach can easily punish the Restless Gambler after the uppercut, catching them while they're using Fever Breaker, and netting you a combo. Another good example is True Cannon's Appetizer; a True Cannon player may think that they're safe attepting to combo extend out of that move from a distance, but typically you can easily catch them with Judgement's Reach due to how long that move's duration is. Even if you don't land the interruption variant and just land the normal first hit, you can side dash immediately and go in for an m1 string. This can catch players off guard (especially against a wall) and lead to huge damage. All in all, Judgement's Reach is a great yet situational poke that has its place in Defense Attorney's kit. Also, [b][i]DO NOT, UNDER NO CIRCUMSTANCE, USE THE "USE TWICE" VARIANT OF THIS MOVE.[/i][/b] The only time you realistically should is if you kill someone with the first hit and want an extra 5 ult bar. Otherwise, 3+3 is inarguably Defense Attorney's worst move in his whole kit. Incredibly unsafe, lackluster reward, wonky hitbox, and very easy to react to, this variant stinks. Even if you land the interruption on the first hit of this variant, a front dash + m1s will always deal more damage. Never use it. Unless you want to style on someone.

[b][i]UNLIKE [/i][/b]its disappointing brother, [i](Judgement's Reach's "Use Twice" variant)[/i] this move is actually a little useful. Sure it's plenty punishable on whiff, but it's also quick enough to be used after No Escape and long enough to net some hits. It's probably not the [i]best[/i] option you have after hitting someone with your No Escape, but with so many options your opponent has to look out for after you land R you can very easily condition them into falling for this move. 4 and all of its variants are all varying degrees of useful for Defense Attorney. All of these variants are great neutral skips and pokes, as they pushback on block and are hard to punish properly. On hit, however, normal 4 cannot true combo into anything. This is where the "mixup-based" part comes into play. After the initial kick, you enter a run where you're free to use 1, 2, or press 4 again to follow up. Remember; none of these options will be true off of the kick, and all of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is why, normally, when you get the opponent in a combo without their evasive, you'll want to just go for R+4 instead as it's a true combo extend that you don't have to risk missing the mixup on. There's only one case which you shouldn't do this, being after R+3, as typically your r will be on cooldown after landing the slam. But when you know your opponent has evasive, it's a lot easier to sneak this move into untrue combos due to its hard to react to startup when compared to R+4, which requires you to throw your mallet beforehand, essentially telling the opponent what you intend to do. For the normal variant (4 or 4+4), it's a risky combo extender/combo starter, and there's 2 ways that you should use this move. 1: Land the first hit of 4, press 4 again IMMEDIATELY when you get within range to avoid getting the move cancelled/dashed out of. 2: Land the first hit of 4, run straight at the opponent and turn around right as you get slightly behind them to cross up their block. This is risky, but the more you go for 4+4 the more opponents will try to anticipate you going for 4+4, which is when you start using the other variants of this move to punish their block. It's also important to note that another use of this move is to net kills; the execution hp requirement is very lenient (around 15 hp), giving this move a huge window where it's an easy kill in neutral given its speed and overall safety.

Probably the least useful follow up from 4 out of the 3, but it still can do some stuff. First of all, most important thing to know when it comes to this move: unlike 4 + 1, this move can be countered AND you can get hit during the windup. It has the benefit of actually dealing damage on hit as a result, but since you just used up 2 of your ragdoll-hitting moves to use this move you aren't really getting that much off of that hit. You can sometimes sneak in a Grapple if you land this against an opponent who doesn't block it, but typically it's better to go for R after on hit to reset your pressure since 4 + 2 > 3 isn't all that consistent. It's definitely not a bad move. It's probably the most "safe" option to go for after 4, since you can't be punished for guessing wrong with it unless they have a counter. But you're not playing this character because you wanna play safe, are you.

With his many mobility options to approach and engage with the enemy, Defense Attorney is able to keep pressuring Honored One, discouraging them from using any pokes such as Reversal Red or Limitless. A well-timed 1+R can and WILL guardbreak a Limitless! However, Defense Attorney only has 90 HP, and Honored One's heavy hitting combos will ensure that even under pressure, they are still a very present threat throughout the fight. If the opponent is aggressive/approaching, Disaster Plants should focus on keeping distance away from melee range and weaving around enemy attacks, to find openings to land her moves safely or counter with flower field. Turning their aggression into an opportunity to combo start. However, if Disaster Plants misses/whiffs one of her moves at this range, it could be devastating, nearly always resulting in any competent opponent landing a combo. Disaster Plants must be careful to not leave themselves vulnerable while still keeping up controlled aggression and pressure on her passive opponents. Rarely will an opponent be purely passive or purely aggressive. A good Disaster Plants should be able to read and adapt to their opponent as the fight changes states.

Plant Guidance's Block-Breaking Spike or Flower Field may be able to circumvent this by hitting/interrupting Honored One as they teleport, but this requires planning ahead since the teleport's windup is significantly faster than both options, making it a situational counter. In close range, it comes down to if Disaster Plants can land [b]Defense Response[/b] or if Honored One can bypass Disaster Plants' block either by[b] side-dashing or using Rapid Punches[/b]. Using[b] Plant Guidance's Flower Field[/b] here is significantly better as you retreat since Honored One doesn't have a way to reliably hit a defensive Disaster Plants with ranged options. To summarise this, Honored One can take advantage of Disaster Plants' long endlag for whiffing while Disaster Plants has few options to defend themselves from that. Against Vessel, Disaster Plants has to worry about the sheer mobility Vessel has, with Aerial Crushing Blow being able to avoid attacks such as Root Swarm and Lasso, while Aerial Cursed Strikes is able to avoid Aerial Defense Response (with a stricter timing). Due to Vessel's aggressive nature, Disaster Plants needs to ensure that they are able to keep pace with them, and respond accordingly. In this matchup, both sides have their own advantages. Vessel can easily approach and dodge the attacks of Disaster Plants. Plant Guidance's Flower Field, which would usually be useful in handling aggressive opponents can be bypassed by Vessel using Aerial Cursed Strikes and Crushing Blow to engage, with the former being unblockable as well. If a Disaster Plants gets desperate and uses Defense Response recklessly, Vessel can use Manji Kick to counter them, effectively wasting Disaster Plants' main keep-away tool. Disaster Plants isn't all hopeless against all this however, Vessel's kit lacks neutral options other than their feinting and M1s, giving Disaster Plants ways to keep away and defend themselves in case a Vessel approaches, like using Root Swarm up close to catch Vessel off-guard, or using Defense Response as a Vessel blocks, which can also lead into a combos. Disaster Plants also has a huge advantage at range (obviously), if a Vessel were to avoid Disaster Plants' attacks from afar, they'd need to react fast enough to either block or dodge certain attacks, if they react wrongly (e.g blocking during Aerial Defense Response, getting caught by Surging Thorns' relatively quick windup), they can easily be placed into combos by Disaster Plants. Plant Guidance can assist in placing Flower Field in case Disaster Plants whiffs an attack, and since Vessel primarily relies on getting close, the usual side-dash M1 would get cancelled, or the Vessel has to reposition to find another opportunity. In short, while Vessel has ways to get up close, it is under the assumption that they are able to react to every single attack that Disaster Plants can dish out, while Disaster Plants does have more options to defend themselves in case the Vessel gets close.

In exchange, Locust Guy sacrifices every single possible neutral application of his skills, leaving only behind Sidedash M1 and a 16s short air dash. Wing Throw is Locust Guy's BEST combo extender, due to it's shorter cooldown, ability to hit on ragdoll, and potential to waste opponent evasive if they use it too early, leading to a full combo. To utilise Wing Throw effectively and set up for Fluttering Pounce Air Combo Variant (R special), you must aim your camera up after grabbing your opponent so that they are thrown higher in order to extend their ragdoll time. However the most useful thing you can do with Wing Throw (that requires a bit of timing) is throwing your opponent directly upwards and as they are falling catch them with an M1, this leads into a full M1 reset and a combo and is fully red, an alternative to this that is easier is Catching them with Clever due to its larger hitbox that lasts longer, which also leads into an M1 reset and combo.

Fluttering Pounce is Locust Guy's only mobility option outside of Side and Front Dashing, Rolling, and Wall Running, and it can be very useful in a mix or combo extend, however its detriment is that it is on a 16s combo when used in neutral, leading it to be a tool that has to be used sparingly. In order to be used as a mixup option, fluttering pounce can be used by aiming up/over the opponent's head, and either side/back dashing to the position you were previously in when closer to the ground, you can bypass lock on and hit behind their block, another option is to jump as you hit the ground for a roll or front dash, acting similarly to what you can do off Vessel feint. Note That pressing an M1 mid Fluttering Pounce will lead to the Pounce being Cancelled by the M1 and stopping all momentum, which can add to the mix by changing up the times at which you stop flying and can side/backdash to change direction or front dash. If timed correctly, pressing M1 Fluttering Pounce in close succession, will lead to an extra M1. This can be done with an uppercut leading to a double uppercut, via: 3xM1 + Uppercut + Look up + Pounce + Hold M1, which can lead to a Pounce Air Combo Variant.

In case of Vessel landing an M1, their options aren't good, their best bet is to use normal Cursed Strikes as quickly as possible to give themselves i-frames and hopefully make you whiff a move, but even then, this move is punishable after it ends by either Ankle Cutter or High Time (this one less consistent), the Aerial version is also punishable by these moves. Counters aren't good against Lucky Coward since the sword counts as an NPC and therefor Manji Kick will counter the air in case of Ankle Cutter and High Time hitting. This is not the case for Dirty Play and Cheap Shot, so keep that in mind.

Puppet Master can be simplified as a pressure cooker, in which his kit revolves around swarming the opponent with his puppets. His unique [color=#4dd2ff]Offload[/color] special allows him to have variants on 3(basically 4) of his base moves and a new move without consuming the move's cooldown and remaining safe. Both Puppet Barrage and Offloaded Ultra Cannon are pressure tools that force opponents to block. Offloaded Ultra Spin and Heat Emission are both neutral tools that can force an opening for a combo, while all other moves like Boost On can be used at any point in a combo to extend. Using the special while it's still on cooldown will instead use [color=#c3063c]Übercharge[/color]. Puppet Master can still use his offloaded moves except Puppet Barrage in this state, but the move will be put on cooldown upon use while requiring 10% of his ultimate bar to use. While this drains a lot of ultimate bar and removes some of his tools for pressure, this can also reward Puppet Master with higher damage in his comboes. Overall, Puppet Master is a very strong character with an abundance of tools at his disposal for any given scenario in a fight. With enough range and safety from his moves, he is one of the top characters in Jujutsu Shenanigans, and will be hard to fight against if even a single hit lands.

Puppet Master general strategy is to use his moves and special to swarm and overload the opponent with pressure in different ways, whether that's to use certain moves to close in for M1s, punishing mistakes, or to keep an opponent at bay with range. If played properly, the opponent is at a disadvantage due to dealing with the threats of both the Puppet Master and the puppets, allowing for easier conversions into comboes. During the start of a game, the first goal is to get around 20-30% of your ultimate bar so you can comfortably start doing the techs Puppet Master has. This can be adjusted higher depending per player.

Boost On can surprise people during M1 trades if you do M1 > Boost On instead of M1 x2, but don't expect this to work more than once or twice on competent players. Offloaded Ultra Spin is also a very useful interruption tool to punish opponents who don't bother to block it after they evasive or try to attempt their combo on the player.

Do keep in mind that they may be given burst if they hit the puppet before you can hit them.

It's just barely dodgable with side dash if you throw it out raw. You can use this move before or after any other move during combos, there is no move this cannot combo into, as long as you aren't too close. Your minimum distance to hit this move is side dash range.

You have to factor in two things when encountering an opponent The preferred playstyle of their character The choices they make to enforce their preferred playstyle The most important factor is the preferred playstyle of their character. You will punish the wrong choices they make to enforce it (i.e. a bad front dash) and prevent the “correct” choices from punishing you. Most playstyles can be broken under two categories: Rushdown and Zoner. The definitions should not be taken too literally, but most characters operate better depending on their range from their opponent. Reggie is the cog in this, as he can be either Rushdown or Zoner. Here is how you should play against these playstyles:

Characters who you should look out for are: Yuji, Naoya, and Todo Since your opponent will always want to approach you, you must counter that. Your most important moves are Gushing Wound, Garage Sale, and Littering. You must use these to keep range. Gushing Wound should always be thrown out in further engagements (when there is more of a distance between you and the opponent) to slow down their approach. Garage Sale does a similar job to Gushing Wound in keeping them out, but can be used in closer engagements to push them away. Littering should be used in a fashion similar to Choso’s Blood Orb that is left behind by Aerial Flowing Red Scale, giving yourself an area where you are immune from combos (you can activate Littering while stunned).

Characters you should look out for are: Ryu, Hanami, and Haruta. Since your opponent wants to stay as far away from you as possible, you must use your pokes and range closing tools to counter that. The most important ones are Gushing Wound, Garage Sale, and Red Seal Speed Crash. Restless Gambler is a scrappy brawler with tools intended to be able to used in almost any situation, which is meant to make him very well-rounded. However, as a result of little to no movement options and a lack of ranged options (outside of Reserve Balls), he ends up being a brawler who rarely gets an opening, making it so that every opportunity he gets must be capitalized on heavily. Restless Gambler gameplay mainly focuses around his second ability, Shutter Doors, as it provides combo extension, move variants, aerial mobility and can create a threat through the use of aerial Rough Energy. His neutral and disadvantage states are terrible due to his lack of good get-off-me tools and pokes, leading him to mainly rely on M1 trades to get much of anything done.

Honored One generally M1 trades better and can invalidate your counter with Reversal Red and intentionally missing his moves. You can counter Rapid Punches after 1R but it can just as easily be baited out for more damage. Honored One Limitless can also catch you out of the air after jumping on shutter doors or during aerial 3, making these options significantly less viable in this matchup.

Use your counter to invalidate any wake-up shenanigans a Honored One player may try with 3. 1+2 can punish Lapse Blue on block and should be one of your main tools in this matchup. Keep the fight grounded, Honored One won't mind you going into the air to use Limitless on you to then lead into a 50/50 with 3.
What should you do versus them?

Restless Gambler generally outclasses Vessel in close combat altercations. Restless Gambler counter is a decent tool in this matchup as Vessel moves are very telegraphed, though he can feint. Although Vessel also has a lower HP pool than Restless Gambler, with some simple combos doing a majority of his HP. Fever Crush, as an example, would do 1/4th of a Vessel's health bar.

Be wary of Vessel's feints. A simple feint can put you into a bad spot, especially after a counter. Manji Kick can counter your Reserve Balls. Avoid trying to combo start with 1+2 as much in this matchup. You can attempt to bait out a Manji Kick by using Reserve Ball and then turning to a slightly different direction.
What should you do versus them?
A ditto is a ditto. Not much else to say here. The most notable thing in this matchup is that you can use aerial 3 to counter their aerial 3.

Dismantle Net -> Dismantle Barrage -> World Cutting Slash -> Disgraced Sovereign Dismantle Net is even stronger than Open Furnace in lethality, so Strongest of History can use Cleave Rush to space himself and then fire it with no consequences. Dismantle Barrage is a great tool to space himself as well, and does great damage of course. It can be led into an Open Furnace or Dismantle Net with minimal risk. Strongest of History can produce this situation rather easily by just using a Dismantle Barrage. After each Black Flash you can backdash and continue to chain to keep yourself safe. Switcher is a character revolving around his burst damage and his swaps. With most of his moves being close range, he's sure to do a lot of damage if an opponent lets him win an engagement, with tools in his disposal to get in their face and start fighting. [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]Boogie Woogie[/color] is his special which can act as a way to dodge, disorient, and feint, but is best used as a catalyst for his variants. He has Swift Kick, which is a kick that comes out moderately fast into a grab that can extend his combos. His third move, Pebble Throw, is a versatile tool that's used best with his special, acting as both an approach tool and a combo extender into a move with high burst damage, like Brute Force. With the combination of his newfound combo potential, as well as an effective approach tool and evasive bait, Switcher is one hard-hitting pick for a character that mostly relies on fundamentals.[color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)][/color]

Switcher's gameplan is to get up close using [i]Pebble Throw[/i], with its two variants: [i]Blazing Star[/i] is the move that allows Switcher to glide around his opponent, letting him hit different angles fast. [i]Gut Punch[/i] is [i]Pebble Throw's[/i] second variant, which either directly puts him in an advantageous position, stunning his opponent and swapping him in front of them, or in a neutral position favored towards him if its blocked due to its low endlag. It's a high priority for Switcher to bait out evasive, as most of his moves have high enough startup to be easily punishable, which can be done with [i]Swift Kick[/i] and [s](again)[/s] [i]Pebble Throw[/i], as [i]Pebble Throw[/i] threatens a 30 damage followup.

The defining trait of Switcher that differentiates him from other characters. Boogie Woogie, with its very low startup up close, can be unpredictable against an opponent during an M1 trade, forcing them to constantly react to his swaps. It also can feint moves at any point during them, allowing him to mitigate his high whiff endlag on his moves, as well as to keep combos true, namely with [i]Elbow Drop[/i]. These are other uses for [color=hsl(180, 100%, 83%)]Boogie Woogie[/color]: Feint mixups Combo extending after using [i]Brute Force[/i] Swapping himself or his opponent to an object made by an opponent (Lucky Coward's sword, Black Death's Earthen Insect Trance, etc.)

He can use Blazing Star, Pebble Throw's variant, to get close with his opponent. Pebble Throw can also be a good interruption tool, with its low startup and its follow-up to Gut punch. He can also use Boogie Woogie during M1 trades, in tandem with sidedashes, to gain a positional advantage. If an opponent burnt their sidedash within sidedash range, he can use sidedash and Elbow Drop as it's unblockable.

Four base moves, two special variant moves, one special with three main variants. Overall a consistent base kit with some stellar tools. [kbd]Swift Kick[/kbd] is your bread and butter combo extender, screwy kick with weird hitboxes then unblockable grab that can setup into every move; [kbd]Pebble Throw[/kbd], [kbd]Brute Force[/kbd], [kbd]Blazing Star[/kbd], and [kbd]Elbow Drop[/kbd]. [kbd]Brute Force[/kbd] is the basic "punch", high damage and knockback, though slow windup, that can still blockbreak with wind. [kbd]Pebble Throw[/kbd] is jack of all trades, movement, combo ender or extender, and mix-up. Stomp then punch out a little pebble you can swap with. [kbd]Elbow Drop[/kbd] is an unblockable launch into the air and slam on the ground. Combo extender that can be used to cheese M1 trades, in the same realm as Rapid Punches.

Blazing Star can be used for movement via using it in neutral, mixup by swapping with the pebble mid move, or use the Black Flash which is STRICTLY a combo ender. (if you can can actually hit it raw send it in the discord) Pebble Combo is used by hitting an opponent with Pebble Throw, it lets you teleport and punch them, with a 1.5s window, to hit your opponent and is generally safe on block even though the punches are blockable.

Boogie Woogie is a clap that swaps the position of you and another. Perfect Swapping is performed by M1ing after a swap, which can restore the cooldown mostly and return the ult cost. Fakeout Swapping is performed by M1ing before a swap, which cancels the swap so no cooldown or ult is consumed. Feint Swapping is performed by swapping mid move which cuts the cooldown of the move in half before the hitboxes come out.

"The act of applause is an acclamation of the soul!" - from the best Switcher main of all time Contest neutral through [kbd]Pebble Throw[/kbd] or [kbd]Swift Kick[/kbd] and win M1 trades through [kbd]Elbow Drop[/kbd]. Try and bait evasive with [kbd]Elbow Drop[/kbd] or [kbd]Swift Kick[/kbd], though more punishable. Generally, combos consist of starting with [kbd]Swift Kick[/kbd] or [kbd]Elbow Drop[/kbd], extending with [kbd]Pebble Throw[/kbd] or [kbd]Swift Kick[/kbd], and ending with [kbd]Brute Force[/kbd]. Utilizing swaps is where you can express yourself. Swap after throwing them an opponent into air with Swift Kick to get a roll into an M1 trade, cancel [kbd]Elbow Drop[/kbd] into [kbd]Blazing Star[/kbd], feint [kbd]Brute Force[/kbd] to draw out counters on get up, the possibilities are limitless.

An [b]Archetype[/b] refers to a character’s [b]optimal playstyle[/b] and [b]type of Neutral[/b] based on their attributes/properties such as movement, move types, neutral tools, gimmicks, combo strength, and the fundamentals. Most importantly, an [b]Archetype[/b] in JJS here is defined in the context of a 1v1 ranked match [i](1v1, no Ult, first to 3, and ranked maps)[/i], so we don’t categorize the characters by their strength in a public server for example or how strong their ult are.
What is an archetype in JJS?

Being a certain Archetype does not mean a bad thing; it just describes their optimal gameplan and the way they interact in the [b]Neutral state[/b] of the game [b]Traditional Archetypes[/b] will be redefined and re-fit to make them make sense within the context of JJS (A Keep Away would not mean sitting halfway across the map sniping people down, etc.)

These characters aren't defined by their effective range but by their ability to bait and punish with their skills [i](For example: Predicting an enemy Side Dash and going in to punish it without the need of Side Dash M1)[/i]. [color=hsl(3, 93%, 63%)]Reversal[/color] is defined by their ability to turn around the flow of the match and to gain great value from correctly guessing and punishing their opponent mistakes. While their capability upclose might be subpar compared to a [color=hsl(217, 91%, 60%)]Close In[/color], their skills and abilities are designed to keep up the pressure at range and zone the opponent out [i](Long Range Blockbreaker, Poke, Trap, Area Denial, etc.)[/i]; then win the [color=hsl(127, 59%, 58%)]Keep Away[/color] the game

Defined by his amazing long ranged capabilities and solid close ranged moves, True Cannon is able to do strong damage from just about any range in a fight. He has access to his defining safe and spammable projectile, Granite Blast, which can be charged to block-break and deal extra damage. Second Helping is a block-break that's extremely difficult for most characters to deal with without a having access to a counter, alongside having moves like Appetizer and Unsatisfied that can lead to devastating combos when landed. Most of these moves come with the cost of having to manage a resource meter, "Overheat". True Cannon has subpar damage when overheated, and does not have access to Granite Blast or most of Appetizer's projectiles without having sufficient meter. This means he can struggle against characters that can close the distance easily when he needs to use his special, which leaves him completely vulnerable. True Cannon does have setups that allow him to somewhat consistently get out of overheat safely, but this doesn't mean that you shouldn't manage your meter to avoid Overheat. Having tools that can completely negate the M1 trading aspect of the game that most characters in the game are forced to engage in, True Cannon is easily one of the top tiers in Jujutsu Shenanigans, with hard to punish weaknesses if your character isn't able to contest his playstyle.

Restless Gambler is characterized by possessing limited effective mobility and a heavy reliance on close quarter combat to score meaningful damage. Being unable to approach against True Cannon is usually an unwinnable matchup for the opposing player. However, Restless Gambler does possess some useful tools for this particular matchup. Restless Gambler's Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant is uniquely suited to punish True Cannon at range. As such, True Cannon's Sweet, Granite Blast, and Appetizer can be punished in certain circumstances. Restless Gambler's Door Guard can be used to counter neutral Second Helping, and block charged Granite Blasts. Unfortunately, the best it can do against Granite Blast is block the attack; the Hakari is still left in punishable endlag. However, if True Cannon plays intelligently, even Restless Gambler's small counterplay can be negated entirely.

In order to take full advantage of Restless Gambler's weak approach capabilities, a True Cannon should stay at range as best they can. Door Guard's ability to block Second Helping can be negated by simply missing the hit of Second Helping as a method of coutnerbaiting. A Restless Gambler with evasive can evasive punish extremely telegraphed attacks from Granite Blast and Appetizer with the Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant. As True Cannon, it is much safer to simply use these moves on a standing Restless Gambler to prevent this from happening. Tracking the cooldown of Restless Gambler's Reserve Balls + Shutter Doors variant can help you decide when it is fully safe to pursue certain combo routes and neutral options.
